```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A Ruscker portal keeps the accounts, the groups and the sign-in of an
organisation in one place. An R web application can rely on it instead
of managing passwords of its own, and `rusckersso` is the small piece
that tells the application **who** is on the other side.

There are two situations, and the package has one half for each.

| Where the app runs | What the app does | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| **Inside** the portal, as one of its hosted apps | Nothing: the portal has already signed the person in and passes their identity along | `hosted_identity()`, `hosted_identity_plumber()` |
| **Outside** the portal, on its own server | Sends the person to the portal to sign in, and checks what comes back | `sso_client()`, `sso_start()`, `sso_finish()` |

Both halves end in the same **identity** object.

```{r setup}
library(rusckersso)
```

## Inside the portal

The portal's proxy adds the person's identity to every request it
forwards to a hosted app, as HTTP headers. The app's entry in the
portal's configuration has to ask for them — nothing is sent by default:

```yaml
add-default-http-headers: true          # the username and the groups
identity-claims: [email, setor, roles]  # optional extras
```

In a Shiny app, the identity is one call inside the server function:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  id <- hosted_identity(session)
  if (is.null(id)) {
    # nobody is signed in (a public app), or the headers are not enabled
  }
}
```

In a plumber2 handler it is `hosted_identity_plumber(request)`.

Here is what comes back, using a stand-in for the Shiny session so the
example runs anywhere:

```{r}
session <- list(request = list(
  HTTP_X_SP_USERID          = "ana",
  HTTP_X_SP_USERGROUPS      = "fiscal,obras",
  HTTP_X_RUSCKER_USER_EMAIL = "ana@example.org",
  HTTP_X_RUSCKER_USER_ROLES = "fiscal:analista,fiscal:gestor"
))

id <- hosted_identity(session)
id
```

Two things worth knowing:

* **Read the identity from the request, never from an environment
  variable.** One container serves many people; an environment variable
  can only ever describe one of them.
* **A value the app sees was put there by the portal.** The proxy removes
  these headers from whatever the visitor's browser sent, so they cannot
  be forged from outside — provided the app is reachable only through
  the portal.

## Asking questions about the identity

What a group or a role *means* is the application's business. The
package only answers the questions:

```{r}
has_group(id, "fiscal")
has_role(id, "fiscal", "gestor")
has_role(id, "obras", "gestor")
roles(id, "fiscal")
```

A typical use is to turn group roles into the application's own
profiles, instead of keeping a table of users:

```{r}
profile <- if (has_role(id, "fiscal", "gestor")) {
  "manager"
} else if (has_group(id, "fiscal")) {
  "analyst"
} else {
  "visitor"
}
profile
```

## Outside the portal

An app on its own server signs people in the way "Sign in with Google"
works: it sends the browser to the portal, the person signs in there,
and the portal sends them back with a one-time code that the app
exchanges for the identity.

First, an Admin of the portal registers the app (**SSO → Clients**) and
gives its developer four values:

```{r}
client <- sso_client(
  issuer        = "https://portal.example.org",   # the portal's address
  client_id     = "my-app",
  client_secret = "from-an-environment-variable", # never in the code
  redirect_uri  = "https://app.example.org/"      # exactly as registered
)
client
```

The sign-in then takes two calls. They need a real portal, so they are
shown but not run here.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# 1. When the person asks to sign in:
start <- sso_start(client)
start$url      # send the browser to this address
start$pending  # keep these three values until the person comes back

# 2. When the portal sends the person back to redirect_uri:
id <- sso_finish(client, session$clientData$url_search, start$pending)
id$sub         # the person's permanent id on the portal
```

`sso_finish()` checks, in this order, and stops at the first problem:
that the portal did not report an error, that the callback belongs to
the sign-in that was started, that it really came from the portal, that
the code can be exchanged, and that the identity token is authentic,
meant for this app, not expired and tied to this sign-in.

Store **`id$sub`** as the key for the person in your own data. A
username can be given to someone else after an account is deleted; the
`sub` cannot.

The package's README has a complete Shiny app built on these two calls.

Two more addresses complete the picture. Neither is run here, the first
because it reads the portal's discovery document:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Signing out: end the app's own session FIRST, then send the browser here.
sso_sign_out_url(client, post_logout_redirect_uri = "https://app.example.org/signed-out")

# The portal's "change your password" page, which links back to the app.
sso_password_url(client)
```

And `sso_start(client, prompt = "none")` checks quietly whether the
person is still signed in to the portal: no page is shown, and someone
who is not comes back with `error=login_required`.

## When a sign-in fails

Every failure is an R condition with its own class, so the app can
react to each case without reading message text. Two of them can be
shown without a portal, because they are detected before anything is
sent over the network.

A callback that does not belong to the sign-in that was started:

```{r}
pending <- list(state = "what-we-stored", nonce = "n", code_verifier = "v")

tryCatch(
  sso_finish(client, "?code=abc&state=something-else", pending),
  rusckersso_state_mismatch = function(e) "This link is not from your sign-in. Start again."
)
```

The portal refusing the person — for instance because they are not in
the groups allowed to use this app:

```{r}
tryCatch(
  sso_finish(client, "?error=access_denied&state=what-we-stored", pending),
  rusckersso_provider_error = function(e) {
    if (identical(e$error, "access_denied")) {
      "You do not have access to this application."
    } else {
      "The sign-in could not be completed."
    }
  }
)
```

Choose your own wording from the error's class or code, as above. Do
not show the error's message to the person as it is: part of it
arrives in the address of the callback, which anyone can craft.

Catching `rusckersso_error` handles every case at once. The full list
is in `?"rusckersso-errors"`.

## What the package does not do

* **Sessions.** After a sign-in the application keeps its own session,
  as it does today.
* **Sign the person out by itself.** Ending the application's session
  is the application's job; `sso_sign_out_url()` only gives the address
  that ends the portal's session afterwards.
* **Deciding permissions.** It reports groups and roles; what they
  allow is up to the application.
